title: Deep-Sea 'Living Fossil' Filmed Alive for the First Time, Shattering Depth Records
summary:
For decades, the goblin shark has been the stuff of deep-sea legend—a bizarre, pink-skinned predator with a protruding snout and extendable jaws, known almost exclusively from dead specimens hauled up by fishermen. Now, in a historic breakthrough, researchers have documented live, healthy goblin sharks thriving in the wild, offering an unprecedented glimpse into the life of one of the ocean's most elusive creatures.

The two sightings, reported in the Journal of Fish Biology, were led by a University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa team. One shark was observed near a seamount close to Jarvis Island in the Central Pacific; the other was recorded along the slope of the Tonga Trench. The Tonga Trench encounter is particularly significant: it occurred nearly 700 meters deeper than any previously known goblin shark habitat, setting a new depth record for the entire order Lamniformes—the group that includes great whites and makos.

'Seeing the most iconic of all the deep-sea sharks alive and looking healthy in its natural habitat is a unique honor,' said lead author Aaron Judah. The discovery also dramatically expands the species' geographic range. Before this, goblin sharks were thought to be confined to pockets off Japan, Australia, and the western US. The new Central Pacific locations suggest a far wider distribution.

Ironically, the first observation almost slipped through the cracks. In 2019, the remotely operated vehicle Hercules recorded footage during an Ocean Exploration Trust expedition, but the shark wasn't identified until Judah reviewed the archived video in 2025. 'I was shocked to hear this because this species was not known to be in the Central Pacific,' he said. A second encounter in 2024, captured by a baited camera during the Inkfish Open Ocean Expedition, confirmed the finding. 'I never thought we'd see a goblin shark alive, and then to do so was amazing,' said co-author Alan Jamieson.

These findings underscore how little we know about the deep ocean. As Judah emphasized, 'New discoveries like this demonstrate that there is still so much to explore.' The expanded range also has practical implications: nations can now include the goblin shark in regional conservation plans. For a species that has survived since the Cretaceous, this new chapter is a reminder that even 'living fossils' can still surprise us.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that huge gaps remain in our knowledge of life on Earth, especially in the deep ocean—a realm that could hold clues to new medicines, biological adaptations, and the history of life. Understanding and protecting such species is crucial as deep-sea mining and climate change threaten these barely explored ecosystems.

background_read: The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, located on Oʻahu island, is a leading center for marine biology and deep-sea research.
The deep sea, defined as waters below 200 meters, covers more than 65% of Earth's surface, yet less than 20% has been mapped in high resolution.
Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) like Hercules, run by the nonprofit Ocean Exploration Trust, have become essential tools for filming life in extreme ocean depths without human risk.
Goblin sharks are part of the order Lamniformes, which also includes the great white and mako sharks, and first appeared in the Cretaceous period over 100 million years ago.
The Tonga Trench, where one shark was spotted, is one of the deepest points in the Pacific Ocean, reaching depths of about 10,800 meters.

perspectives.description: The sightings are a triumph for marine biology, proving that elusive creatures can be studied without harming them or their habitat. This non-invasive research method could be a model for studying other deep-sea species. It also gives hope that conservation efforts can be informed by direct observation rather than dead specimens.

However, the fact that goblin sharks were found in new regions also highlights how little we know—and how much could be destroyed before we even discover it. Deep-sea mining and pollution may already be affecting habitats we haven't even begun to understand. The species' survival since the Cretaceous no guarantee against modern human pressures.

The record depth for Lamniformes challenges assumptions about the physiological limits of sharks in high-pressure environments. It also raises questions about how isolated populations are and whether the Central Pacific sharks are genetically distinct. The lag between recording and identification demonstrates the enormous backlog of unexplored deep-sea footage.

Going forward, more targeted deep-sea expeditions, using cheap baited cameras and AI video analysis, could uncover many more 'lost' sightings hidden in archives. If goblin sharks are indeed widespread, international cooperation will be needed to protect their habitat across national boundaries. This could spur the creation of high-seas marine protected areas.
